title: Your Neighbor Matters: Towards Fair Decisions Under Networked Interference

problem.claim: Decision-making in social networks can introduce bias because individuals are interconnected and decisions may depend on neighbors' sensitive attributes.

gap.claim: Conventional fairness approaches often assume independent individuals and overlook how one person's sensitive attribute affects others' decisions.

contributions.claim: Introduces Interference-aware Fairness (IAF) with Self-Fairness and Peer-Fairness as two forms of discrimination.
Defines network-informed decisions as fair only when Self-Fairness and Peer-Fairness are satisfied simultaneously.
Develops a deep doubly robust framework to estimate and regularize Self-Fairness and Peer-Fairness metrics for decision models.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate their concepts and methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: Networked decision-making can create bias, including in decisions influenced by neighbors' sensitive attributes.
Existing fairness approaches overlook interference between individuals' sensitive attributes and decisions.
IAF distinguishes self-caused and peer-caused discrimination through Self-Fairness and Peer-Fairness.
Fairness requires satisfying both Self-Fairness and Peer-Fairness simultaneously.
A deep doubly robust framework estimates and regularizes the metrics, with reported validation on synthetic and real-world datasets.

unknowns: Formal definitions of the Self-Fairness and Peer-Fairness metrics are not provided.
The abstract does not specify datasets, baselines, quantitative results, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not establish computational cost, implementation details, or limitations.
